newsitem.title: USA: Legal jargon dominates White House defenses.
newsitem.headline: Legal jargon dominates White House defenses.

text.p: Faced with the daily drip-drip-drip of campaign finance revelations, President Clinton and his White House are resorting to a time-worn Washington tradition to defend their actions -- legal jargon.
It is a practice perhaps best defined by the late Sam Ervin, the courtly North Carolina senator who headed the Senate investigation into the Watergate scandal.
"If a law's against you, you pound the evidence," he advised lawyers. "If the evidence is against you, you pound the law. If both are against you, you pound the table."
Clinton and his aides have been doing a lot of pounding of all varieties in the face of charges on the way Democrats raised money to finance last year's election campaigns.
Vice President Al Gore, a law school dropout, gave the best example of lawyerly defence, based on the advice of his lawyer, in admitting he solicited campaign contributions from his office.
This had raised the question of whether he had violated a law barring solicitation of campaign money while on federal property. He found a loophole.

"My counsel advises me that there is no controlling legal authority or case that says that there was any violation of law whatsoever in the manner in which I asked people to contribute to our re-election campaign," he said.

Lest that message did not sink in, Gore repeated it seven times during the course of a 24-minute news conference. In plain English he meant that there was no test case in court that created a legal precedent.
Conservative columnist Charles Krauthammer called it "one of the flimsiest legal confections of our time."
A couple of days later White House spokesman Mike McCurry was asked whether Clinton himself had made any calls from the White House seeking campaign donations.
McCurry, stung in recent months by offering sweeping statements that turned out to be untrue, gave a qualified response that Clinton "doesn't have any recollection of it."
At a news conference Friday, Clinton said he told McCurry to be ambiguous because he was not sure if he had made any solicitations out of all the phone conversations he had.
"I told him not to flat out say that I'd never done it because I simply can't say that I've never done it. But it's not what I like to do and it wasn't a practice of mine," he said.
Clinton, a former law school professor, made an extremely nuanced explanation of why he thought Gore was not in the wrong by making the phone calls.

"It's clear that what the law is on this, going back a long time, is it's as if he'd written a letter to somebody from the White House. Did the solicitation occur when he wrote the letter or when the letter is received? And the law is clearly that the solicitation is consummated, if you will, when the person is solicited, and where the person is solicited," he said.

More careful legalistic language was used to defend Maggie Williams, the chief of staff to first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton, after it emerged that Williams had accepted a $50,000 political donation from California businessman Johnny Chung while he was visiting the White House in March 1995.
Federal law bars government employees from accepting campaign contributions on government property.

The White House insisted that technically, Williams did not break the law. Although she took the money and turned it over to the Democratic National Committee, she did not "accept" or "receive" it under the definition of the law, officials insisted.
Then there was the question of White House coffees with Clinton. Were people invited to them expected to make campaign contributions?
"As far as we are aware, no one was required to make a contribution, or to commit to do so, in order to attend these White House events," said a recent White House statement.
